#5925. America Can Do Good—and Do Well

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

ANDREW NATSIOS was Administrator of the U.S. Agency for International Development and the President’s Special Envoy to Sudan during the George W. Bush administration. He is the author of Guns Are Not Enough: Foreign Aid in the National Interest, from which this essay is adapted.

Among all the ruinous consequences of the so-called U.S. Department of Government Efficiency’s efforts to cut bureaucracy, none has been as profound as the destruction of the United States’ ability to deliver foreign aid. A comprehensive Lancet study shows that the U.S. Agency for International Development’s assistance prevented more than 90 million deaths between 2001 and 2021. Using a mortality model, Boston University epidemiologist Brooke Nichols has estimated that the 2025 dismantling of USAID contributed to more than 700,000 excess deaths over roughly a year. A study published in Science this May found that after USAID’s shutdown, places that had lost large amounts of the agency’s assistance experienced a marked uptick in armed clashes and riots. The development economists Marcella Nicolini and Fabio Sabatini, meanwhile, showed that economic activity in areas that formerly enjoyed substantial U.S. aid had dramatically declined.

No country can be a great power without a functioning foreign aid program. But today, the United States does not have one. After 90 percent of USAID’s programs were terminated and 90 percent of its staff members were laid off, Congress formally reappropriated most of the budgetary funding dedicated to U.S. foreign aid. But the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) has not released all of this appropriated funding. More damaging still, USAID’s mechanisms for spending aid money have been dismantled. According to the Pew Research Center, annual U.S. foreign aid disbursements fell by $26 billion between the 2023–24 and 2024–25 fiscal years; $2.5 billion in appropriated funding designated for foreign aid went unspent by the end of the 2025–26 fiscal year.

Russell Vought, OMB’s director and a self-identified Christian nationalist, has stonewalled spending for programs related to supporting democracy and insisted that humanitarian grants can be sent only to two specific Christian nongovernmental organizations. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, announced that he wanted to end funding to USAID development contractors, universities, and local civil society organizations without understanding the downside of other options for aid dollars, such as budget support, which are far less accountable, uniquely American, and results-oriented.

Given the suffering created by the end of USAID, it is even more troubling that DOGE’s objectives to slash waste and boost transparency have not been realized. U.S. President Donald Trump’s 2025 “big beautiful bill” erased any modest savings won by DOGE’s cuts to foreign aid. And the decision to move USAID’s functions to the State Department, which has weak business systems and inadequate staff to manage aid programs, has thus far led to the transfer of $3.8 billion in U.S. foreign aid money to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs and $15.9 billion directly into foreign governments’ treasuries through memorandums of understanding.

These governments often have limited capacity to spend the money wisely and produce results. In the past, USAID’s Office of the Inspector General has harshly criticized such options because it is nearly impossible to audit the transfers. Over 90 percent of the countries involved in these agreements score below 50 (out of 100) on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index, indicating serious systemic corruption. This may explain why State Department political appointees have kept the texts of these health agreements secret.

Clashing demands—that aid should relieve misery abroad, that it ought to serve U.S. military and diplomatic interests, and that it ought to yield rapid, visible, and quantifiable results—always complicated the enterprise. And over the course of 65 years since USAID’s 1961 founding, overregulation, a centralization of control over programs, and congressional meddling created a rigid straitjacket that made the United States less responsive to local governments and local needs. But what the current U.S. administration didn’t understand was that USAID’s bureaucracy, so often presented as an obstacle to effectiveness, was in fact an adaptation to manage these conflicts.

Simply abolishing that institutional architecture with no plan to replace it has only generated more confusion and waste. Meanwhile, China is racing to offer alternative sources of development financing, and Russia is seeking to expand its global influence through security partnerships. The United States cannot afford to let its foreign aid apparatus atrophy. It must redirect it, not reject aid.

Ever since USAID was created, the expectations that leaders in Washington had for foreign aid have conflicted with realities in the developing world, the way actual aid programs are managed, and the speed and nature of societal change. When I read through USAID’s 1960s-era archives to write my new book, I was struck that the demands early U.S. policymakers made of the institution were the same as those made today: policymakers wanted rapid, visible, and quantifiable results. Those demands were as unrealistic then as they are now. U.S. President John F. Kennedy hoped that poverty in Latin America would visibly recede within a couple of years of USAID’s creation, as he was understandably worried that the Cuban revolutionary leader Fidel Castro’s Marxist ideology was spreading across the region. Fourteen months after the organization’s inception, an article by Joseph Kraft in Harper’s Magazine reported that policymakers in Washington had already judged it a failure because it was not delivering “quick and visible results.” David Bell, USAID’s second administrator, recalled in 1965 that Kennedy had complained that the agency was “slow-moving, inefficient, and unresponsive to the President’s policy.”

But diplomacy and development operate on profoundly different time horizons. Nearly all foreign aid programs have diplomatic consequences, even if they aren’t designed to. When diplomatic goals become the main or only goals of an aid program, however—for instance, when U.S. aid kept the Congolese dictator Mobutu Sese Seko in power during the Cold War—good development often fails.

The United States began institutionalizing foreign aid after World War II through agencies and programs such as the Marshall Plan, which supported the postwar economic recovery of Western Europe, and the Point Four Program, a Truman administration initiative to promote development in poor countries to reduce their susceptibility to communism. All along, policymakers debated whether U.S. assistance programs should principally aim to save lives and reduce extreme poverty or to support U.S. foreign policy by countering the influence of hostile powers.

In fact, USAID ended up playing a key role in winning the Cold War. American assistance strengthened governments targeted for Soviet and Chinese communist subversion, particularly in Asia. After U.S. President Richard Nixon entered his second year in office, aid spending for agriculture was increased to 50 percent of USAID’s budget and was directed primarily toward Asia. According to multiple studies by development economists, the effort saved more than 245 million lives. The green revolution, implemented over decades in Pakistan, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, South Korea, and Taiwan (among other countries), helped produce large grain surpluses that fueled industrialization and economic growth and averted the kind of famines that historically produce coups or mass uprisings.

Throughout this era, however, Washington’s demands that aid accomplish diplomatic goals—and quickly and visibly—also undermined the most important elements of development programs: institution building and policy reform. Strong institutions separate wealthy countries from poor ones. The former have them in abundance, while the latter do not. Institution building and policy reform should be the focus of aid programs. But institution building and policy reform is difficult to measure, takes many years to implement successfully, and is not immediately visible. Instead, policymakers insisted that USAID do service delivery, producing valuable humanitarian programs that were ultimately unsustainable.

Most critical analyses of U.S. foreign aid conclude that USAID came to focus on process over substance, resulting in excessive bureaucracy. What these critiques overlook is what caused this obsessive focus on process. A web of federal regulatory and oversight agencies (what scholars call the counterbureaucracy) loosed on U.S. aid programs an army of federal auditors, accountants, regulators, compliance officers, and congressional staffers dedicated to reining in the bureaucracy and—supposedly—protecting taxpayers’ money. This onslaught slowed down USAID’s implementation of programs and created massive amounts of paperwork. It did not make aid programs more effective.

Historically, Congress ended up playing a particularly intrusive role in the management of U.S. foreign aid programs. USAID reported to 14 congressional committees, which often clashed, pulling USAID in different directions and slowing program implementation. (For example, the House and Senate agriculture committees, under the influence of the agriculture lobby, stonewalled efforts to reform food aid by insisting it be exported from the United States, while legislative appropriators and authorizers from foreign affairs committees strongly supported local purchase reform.) Congress also imposed intrusive earmarks—defined amounts allocated for specific programs, projects, or organizations. When countries asked for specific help, USAID often could not respond, because the glut of earmarks meant there was no discretionary money left.

Starting in the 1990s, the State Department attempted to exert more control over the USAID budget. A 1998 statute, for instance, made the USAID administrator report directly to the secretary of state. In January 2001, the State Department took control of USAID’s budget. That only led lawmakers—who often distrusted State—to add more earmarks. To protect U.S. foreign aid programs from an especially hostile Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman, Republican Senator Jesse Helms, the Clinton administration instructed each cabinet-level department to create its own aid programs that would fall outside that committee’s jurisdiction. For example, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention at the Department of Health and Human Services established regional offices around the world, the Environmental Protection Agency developed solar energy projects in poor countries, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency signed agreements with more than 28 developing countries to assist in disaster management. USAID was already running programs such as these, yielding overlapping mandates which added to the incoherence of U.S. foreign aid.

When I became USAID administrator in 2001, I discovered a foreign aid program whose funds were straitjacketed by nearly 250 congressional earmarks, a sum exceeding USAID’s total appropriation. At the time, Ethiopia was one of the most severely food insecure countries in the world. Yet in 2007 only 1.5 percent of USAID’s budget was devoted to agricultural development, 1.5 percent to economic growth, and 1.5 percent to governance reform; Congressional earmarks made it impossible to fund these programs to match the Ethiopian government’s request.

Despite all these impediments, foreign aid remained a critical component of U.S. foreign policy. The Department of Defense had a particularly productive partnership with USAID, recognizing that foreign aid could be as important as force in incentivizing insurgents to make peace. The effects of USAID projects in Afghanistan were profound but took shape over long time horizons neither the State Department nor the Defense Department had any patience for. (USAID’s Afghanistan media-development program, for instance, was a great success, as documented in a Harvard Kennedy School study by The New York Times’s David Rohde.) Major academic studies have shown that in Iraq, community development projects undertaken by USAID’s Office of Transition Initiatives (OTI) employed large numbers of young men who might otherwise have been recruited into militias, reducing U.S. military casualties in the provinces with the highest levels of violence. In 2004, Army General Peter Chiarelli called the USAID officer managing the program, Kirk Day, a “hero” for saving his soldiers’ lives.

The DOGE team abolished OTI last year, along with innumerable other programs that alleviated suffering globally and enhanced U.S. soft power. When Congress restored many cuts to foreign aid, it did not reinstate USAID’s veteran staff, historical archives, business systems, field presence, or implementing partner networks of universities, international nongovernmental organizations, local civil society groups, and international development contractors. The transfer of programs to the Department of State only exacerbated the contradictions that have long bedeviled U.S foreign aid. Few secretaries of state (or secretaries of defense) have any development background, experience, or technical knowledge, and paradoxically, when aid is seen simply as a tool of diplomacy or defense rather than an end in itself, the diplomatic good it can do is compromised.

Dismantling USAID did not abolish the need for technically knowledgeable staff and bureaucratic systems. In May 2025, the State Department inspector general issued an intimidating report detailing what the department will have to do to competently manage foreign aid programs, a list of demands it will have difficulty meeting. And in September this year, the Government Accountability Office issued a highly critical audit of the State Department’s inadequate management of foreign aid programs, finding that the department lacked documented standards for deciding which aid programs to terminate, could not produce data on its own staffing, and maintained incomplete or incorrect records on grants and agreements. This result was unsurprising, given that the State Department is a diplomatic policy institution, not a program management agency. Merging USAID into the State Department makes as much sense as merging Microsoft with ExxonMobil, given the disparate time horizons on which the two institutions operate and their differences in mission statements and business systems.

The State Department has pursued alternative arrangements for distributing aid that require less direct management. For example, it has negotiated 36 memorandums of understanding with governments in developing countries to transfer U.S. aid funds to their health ministries, so they can spend the program money themselves. But in return for these transfers, Washington has asked these countries to send private health-care data to the U.S. government, accept undocumented immigrants the U.S. government deports, and, in some cases, give U.S. mining companies access to their rare-earth minerals. Because health programs save lives, they should be distributed based on need, not on parochial, transactional American demands.

Many countries have understandably resisted this kind of bargain. USAID had technical staff that could assess a foreign government’s ability to manage funds responsibly. In practice, it ran a detailed and thorough vetting of nearly every aspect of the governments it partnered with. The State Department, by contrast, only vets according to the legal minimum and treats foreign governments as it treats as international or U.S.-based NGOs. State’s approach will increase the risk that funds are stolen by local government ministries that lack the control systems needed to ensure accountability.

The very public and grossly inaccurate attacks on USAID’s integrity and management by Trump and DOGE’s erstwhile leader, Elon Musk, have damaged the agency’s reputation so extensively that simply resurrecting it will be difficult. But Washington’s aid apparatus also needs more coherent organization than it was afforded in the past. In his celebrated work Bureaucracy, on which my book is structured, the political scientist James Q. Wilson argues that strong U.S. departments or agencies need “relative autonomy”: clearly defined missions they do not substantially share with other agencies. By this logic, if the United States wants a high-functioning, coherent foreign aid program, it must first consolidate all aid functions within one department.

Abolishing field offices (called USAID missions) also made administering aid programs much more difficult, blunted true accountability and U.S. influence in the developing world, and reduced the visibility of U.S. aid programs. These country missions must be reestablished, reporting to the local U.S. ambassador. In Washington, Congress should create a new cabinet-level department reporting to the president that manages all the government’s aid programs, which would make it possible to trim staff, streamline program implementation, and avoid policy incoherence. At least 80 percent of this new department’s staff should be deployed abroad, not in Washington. The United States will always need to be able to launch aid programs with an expressly diplomatic purpose and short time horizon, and the State Department should determine these projects and their spending levels. But it should leave the programs’ management up to the new aid department—as it did during the Cold War, when USAID was independent of State.

This new department should also report to fewer congressional committees—a foreign affairs authorizing committee and an appropriations subcommittee in each legislative body. The practice of burdening the United States’ foreign aid budget with domestically appealing earmarks—which prevents aid from responding to foreign countries’ own needs—must be reduced.

In the past, the overregulation and bureaucratization of foreign aid driven by the demands of the counterbureaucracy prioritized process over programs and compliance over developmental outcomes. The new aid department must be given regulatory relief. One way to do that is for Congress to set up charter missions, similar to charter schools, as an experiment to see whether accountability deteriorates. These deregulated charter missions would be free from burdensome reporting requirements the counterbureaucracy demands. In recent years, the World Bank has tried a similar approach and found that it improved its programs’ effectiveness without increasing fraud.

The status quo for U.S. foreign aid cannot last. But Washington cannot revert to the old status quo, which generated the kind of dissatisfactions among policymakers that helped lead to its dismantling. Now is the time to bring more coherence to U.S. foreign aid programs with these reforms, if the new Democratic Congress and future administrations show a forward-looking vision.

Trump Should Refashion the Foreign Aid Agency, Not Dismantle It

#5924. U.S.-China Investments Can Still Work for Americans

Analysis: U.S.-China Investments Can Still Work for Americans

The Board of Trade and Board of Investment, the mechanisms for negotiating tariff reductions and cross-border investment, respectively, were meant to turn the 2025 Busan summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping into concrete economic deliverables. So far, only the Board of Trade has developed an agenda, reflecting how difficult cross-border investment has become amid U.S.-China strategic rivalry.

The Board of Investment could take the easy route of approving a handful of small, nonsensitive deals. Or it could aim higher, pursuing investments that deliver meaningful gains for both countries.

The Board of Trade and Board of Investment, the mechanisms for negotiating tariff reductions and cross-border investment, respectively, were meant to turn the 2025 Busan summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping into concrete economic deliverables. So far, only the Board of Trade has developed an agenda, reflecting how difficult cross-border investment has become amid U.S.-China strategic rivalry.

The Board of Investment could take the easy route of approving a handful of small, nonsensitive deals. Or it could aim higher, pursuing investments that deliver meaningful gains for both countries.

China faces weak demand and fierce competition in its electric-vehicle sector at home. The United States needs more affordable green autos and stronger domestic capabilities in next-generation automotive technologies. At least in theory, some well-designed investment partnerships could help address both sides’ challenges.

Yet much of the current debate rests on misconceptions about what makes China’s EV industry competitive and what the United States stands to gain. The popular proposal is that the United States can ask China to transfer its battery technology and that this would be the magic pill for U.S. EVs. But battery tech is the wrong focus, tech transfer is the wrong approach, and U.S. EVs are the wrong target.

Access to China’s cheaper lithium-ion battery technology would not be enough to make EVs affordable in the United States. Batteries alone will not suffice. Japan and South Korea once led in lithium-ion batteries, yet that advantage did not translate into leadership in EVs.

Chinese automakers came from behind because of their increasingly capable battery suppliers and because they advanced quickly in another, less visible technological foundation: electrical and electronic architecture (EEA), which is the brain and nervous system of an intelligent electric vehicle. Traditional cars rely on hundreds of electronic control units. A software-defined vehicle instead uses a more centralized, zonal architecture in which a few computers coordinate the whole vehicle.

Zonal EEA shortens development cycles, simplifies supply chains, lowers costs, integrates intelligent features, and enables a smartphone-like user experience. Tesla pioneered zonal EEA in 2017, but fierce competition pushed Chinese automakers to catch up quickly.

Nor should the United States try to catch up with China’s well-known lead in EV manufacturing. The acquisition of Chinese technology for battery-electric vehicles (BEVs) is currently a U.S. policy priority, but a lesser-known fact is that China now leads across a broad range of powertrains, including BEVs, plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), and many others.

In fact, going fully electric may not be the best option in the United States. Americans drive roughly twice as many miles each year as Europeans and 70 percent more per passenger car than Chinese, and extending BEV range requires even larger and heavier batteries.

China-developed affordable PHEVs can travel about 100 miles on electricity, enough for most daily commutes, while achieving fuel economy of roughly 60 miles per gallon on longer trips. Limited public charging remains a hurdle for BEVs in the United States. Many suburban homeowners, however, can install home chargers that are more than adequate for the smaller batteries in PHEVs and for routine commuting. Competitive PHEVs, one of China’s technological strengths, are a much better option for serving American consumers facing both rising vehicle prices and higher fuel costs.

Technology transfer could also be a surprising dead end for the United States. Technology transfer is sensitive, as China is not willing to give away the crown jewels of its technology so easily. But even for legacy technology, there is another challenge. If competitive EVs required only batteries, the main task would indeed be getting battery production technology from China.

But making the U.S. auto industry competitive also requires advanced EEA and powertrain technologies. A broader scope of technological domains requires much more than manufacturing know-how; it also requires new supply-chain arrangements and new approaches to research and development. These are beyond the scope of a conventional joint venture, direct investment, or technology license. Asking China to transfer fancy tech is a pipe dream.

The correct approach is what we call deep-tech iterative learning. China’s own experience shows why local manufacturing is insufficient for this. When China set out to modernize its auto industry, policymakers assumed that localized manufacturing of advanced products would automatically build domestic capabilities.

During the 1980s, China experimented with several forms of partnership with international automakers, including joint ventures and technology-licensing arrangements. The result was a mixed bag, with many producing very little transfer. One example was Volkswagen, which did improve Chinese capabilities in manufacturing, supply-chain management, and quality control, but it did relatively little to build domestic R&D.

A second wave of more carefully designed partnerships in the 1990s, especially with General Motors (GM) and Ford, created a more disciplined, step-by-step process for iterative learning in automotive R&D. Over time, the exchange became reciprocal. China acquired technology and engineering expertise. As Chinese partners grew more capable, they helped U.S. automakers improve vehicle quality and reliability while reducing R&D costs after the 2008 financial crisis.

Bargaining power for iterative technological gains comes from leverage, incentives that make technology transfer worthwhile for the provider, and the architecture to make it work. The United States must develop these by doing the hard work: starting small, building new capabilities along the way, and making the next, more substantial step in technology transfer a good deal for both countries, so that it can last for the long haul.

Back then, China’s main bargaining chip was controlled access to its market. In the early 1990s, officials in Shanghai were frustrated by the limited transfer of R&D capabilities from Volkswagen. They negotiated with more than 10 international automakers and ultimately invited GM, Ford, and Toyota into the final bidding process.

China was offering one of the last opportunities for entry before its expected accession to the World Trade Organization around 2001, and Shanghai used competition among bidders to demand strong commitments to localized engineering and R&D. Automakers expected the market to grow multifold to a market comparable to the U.S. one. It eventually became more than twice as big.

GM submitted the strongest offer and won. Its centerpiece was the Pan Asia Technical Automotive Center (PATAC), a joint design and engineering center that became the institutional channel for transferring R&D capabilities and technical knowledge from GM’s global operations to Shanghai.

Deep technology transfer didn’t happen at once. Initially, PATAC’s work was limited to calibrating existing designs and making cosmetic changes. The incentives changed as China overtook the United States to become the world’s largest new-car market in 2009.

China was also a market with distinctive demands. Government and business executives often traveled with larger entourages, creating an unusual demand for premium minivans. Engineers in China also developed a closer understanding of consumers in emerging markets than counterparts in Michigan or at GM subsidiaries in Germany and Australia.

Local knowledge about a distinctive, large market eventually propelled GM to move two major R&D projects into China. The first was a Chinese-developed Buick premium minivan that differed fundamentally from aging GM minivans for American soccer moms. With GM’s support, PATAC engineers learned how to design new vehicle architecture for the first time.

The second was a project with SAIC, its Shanghai partner, to codevelop small engines for global emerging markets, allowing SAIC engineers to develop engines from the ground up. These two programs have sustained sales of millions of units for GM across the world. Engineers trained through these programs later carried their technological knowledge into numerous Chinese carmakers.

With support from central leaders, Shanghai offered foreign automakers a coveted chance to enter a potentially enormous market. China’s distinctive consumer needs, some shared with other emerging markets, gave U.S. automakers commercial reasons to transfer R&D capabilities and know-how. But leverage and incentives produced deeper, long-term iterative learning only when embedded in durable institutions: a manufacturing joint venture and a joint R&D center that could survive shifting political whims.

The United States today has a combination of leverage and incentives like those China possessed. Its market is huge and still largely lacking in affordable electrified models. Chinese automakers, facing thin profit margins at home, are drawn to this untapped demand. The U.S. market is also distinctive in its road conditions, urban form, safety regulations, and consumer preferences.

Chinese companies cannot simply transplant existing blueprints. To build durable, low-maintenance vehicles suited to American roads, they would need to hire and train engineers in the United States, bring key suppliers, and develop capabilities there, much as Japanese automakers did decades ago.

A regulated mechanism such as the Board of Investment could provide the missing institutional structure. Taking baby steps toward transferring some low-hanging-fruit technologies across a broad range, including batteries, EEA, and hybrid powertrains, is neither fanciful nor unrealistic.

If the United States does nothing, it will lose out not just to China but to everyone else. Volkswagen, Mercedes, Renault, as well as Abu Dhabi’s CYVN, have all been working with Chinese firms in different ways to tap Chinese expertise in EEA and powertrain technologies. Toyota is likewise testing cutting-edge EV technologies in China rather than Japan.

The Board of Investment could organize a competitive bidding process to identify Chinese partners with the strongest capabilities and the clearest commitments to participate. Working with one or more interested U.S. automakers, it could invite qualified Chinese firms to compete on the substance of their offers, as Shanghai did 30 years ago.

It would also help if the board devoted more energy to institution-building, including, but not limited to, involving deep industry expertise in assessing and calibrating licensing or joint-venture terms, establishing security guardrails for connected-vehicle technologies, and creating joint R&D institutions modeled on the PATAC so that technical capabilities are continuously channeled into the United States, independent of political favor or goodwill.

National security would be addressed at the technical level, regardless of whether it is prioritized politically. Working first with a select group of Chinese firms to develop and produce smaller battery-electric or plug-in hybrid vehicles in the United States and building from there could be an easy first step.

It sounds complicated, but it’s nothing new. Amid the U.S.-Japan trade tensions, the GM-Toyota joint venture NUMMI (1984) and Toyota (1977) and Honda’s (1975) R&D centers in the United States brought technological capabilities to U.S. automakers, parts suppliers, and engineers.

This is a proven process. U.S. industrial competitiveness, Americans’ everyday quality of life, consumer affordability, and U.S. innovation leadership in general are at stake. Getting it wrong would be tremendously costly.

Lizzi C. Lee is a fellow on Chinese economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis.

Fengming Lu is a lecturer (assistant professor) in the Coral Bell School of Asia Pacific Affairs at the Australian National University.

#5923. Van Hollen challenges Schumer for Senate leadership after Democratic election sweep

Several newly-elected Democratic senators suggest they are not committed to supporting Sen. Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader. Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the Democratic Party’s priorities and leadership plans as Congress prepares to return to session.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., officially has a challenger for the mantle of Democratic leader, and incoming majority leader, in the Senate.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who has become a progressive darling and outlet for those against Schumer’s bid for another term as top Democrat, officially announced that he was jumping in to challenge the longtime figurehead of the Senate Democratic Caucus.

"In this election, the American people called for change," Van Hollen said in a statement. "They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies – but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people."

BERNIE SANDERS SAYS HE WON'T BACK SCHUMER AS PUSH FOR NEW LEADERSHIP GAINS STEAM

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, speaks during a news conference following a Maryland delegation meeting at the U.S. Capitol in Washington on Thursday, June 25, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," he continued. "This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader."

Van Hollen, 67, has served in Congress for 23 years, first starting in the House before moving to the Senate in 2017. Schumer, 75, has been an elected official since 1981.

The Maryland Democrat’s decision to run against Schumer comes after a listening tour with Senate Democrats, and follows his initial ambition of "kicking the tires" on jumping into the 2028 presidential conversation.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: A USER’S MANUAL TO UPCOMING LEADERSHIP ELECTIONS IN THE HOUSE AND SENATE

Since entering the Senate, Van Hollen has occupied Schumer’s left flank. It wasn’t until earlier this week that he fully took a shot at him, arguing that the longtime leader had chosen the "crypto industry," and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) over progressive candidates that eventually won during this past midterm cycle.

But he's managed to capture some of the superstars of the Left, most notably Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who pushed Van Hollen to run.

"The American public spoke clearly last week. They rejected Trumpism. But we have yet to earn our mandate. That will require bold leadership. I called on Sen. [Chris Van Hollen] to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience. We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority."

RACHEL MADDOW WELCOMES 'BIG FIGHT' BETWEEN SOCIALIST AND MODERATE DEMOCRATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks during a press conference at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee headquarters on Nov. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Tom Brenner/Getty Images)

Schumer did not take the challenge lying down.

"I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead," Schumer said on X. "I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader."

"I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people," he continued.Neither did his allies. Schumer has maintained since Democrats flipped the Senate that he would be the one to lead them over the next two years. And one of his possible lieutenants, Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who is vying to replace Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., as Democratic whip, is riding with him through the storm. "Senate Democrats had historic victories last week, thanks to our talented candidates and the hard work of our caucus, led by Senator Schumer. And it was not the first time he has led this caucus back to the majority," Schatz said in a statement.

"The American people sent a clear message: they want us to lower costs, end a needless war, and fight corruption. Our caucus has the right to have a conversation about the path ahead, but we have no time to waste," he continued. "We must move quickly to vote, unify, and get to work. I endorse Senator Schumer for leader and will be voting for him in the caucus election."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

#5920. Russia’s Cheapest Weapon in Its Hybrid War Is Fear

Analysis: Russia’s Cheapest Weapon in Its Hybrid War Is Fear

Understanding the conflict four years in.

On the morning of Nov. 11, some 6,000 Italian schools received an identical email from a “Mikhail Andropov.” A “powerful explosive device with a remote trigger” had been left inside the building, the message said, and the survivors would be finished off with knives. Principals evacuated students from Trieste to Palermo. That same morning, more than 300 schools in Northern Ireland also received threatening emails, and police in Scotland reported similar bomb threats, as well. By midday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had convened an emergency meeting with Italy’s intelligence services and National Cybersecurity Agency at Palazzo Chigi in Rome. No bombs were found.

Five days earlier, emails bearing the same signature and subject line (“Message to the West”) reached newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria, leading the Irish public broadcaster RTE to evacuate its offices and suspend programming. The emails claimed responsibility for a wave of false threats that, between Nov. 3 and Nov. 6, targeted at least 35 passenger flights across Europe. On Nov. 5 alone, around 20 civilian aircraft were affected: Italian, French, and Bulgarian fighter jets scrambled to escort airliners, and an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a French military air base. Italian schools had already been targeted on Oct. 19 and again on Nov. 2, when an email with the same text reached nearly 280 education facilities. In October, hundreds of schools in Britain, Hungary, and Serbia received similar threats.

Principals evacuated students from Trieste to Palermo. That same morning, more than 300 schools in Northern Ireland also received threatening emails, and police in Scotland reported similar bomb threats, as well. By midday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had convened an emergency meeting with Italy’s intelligence services and National Cybersecurity Agency at Palazzo Chigi in Rome. No bombs were found.

Five days earlier, emails bearing the same signature and subject line (“Message to the West”) reached newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria, leading the Irish public broadcaster RTE to evacuate its offices and suspend programming. The emails claimed responsibility for a wave of false threats that, between Nov. 3 and Nov. 6, targeted at least 35 passenger flights across Europe. On Nov. 5 alone, around 20 civilian aircraft were affected: Italian, French, and Bulgarian fighter jets scrambled to escort airliners, and an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a French military air base. Italian schools had already been targeted on Oct. 19 and again on Nov. 2, when an email with the same text reached nearly 280 education facilities. In October, hundreds of schools in Britain, Hungary, and Serbia received similar threats.

Some European intelligence officials consider Russia the most likely origin based on motive, modus operandi, and precedent. At the same time, these officials warn that a firm attribution may never come. Naturally, Moscow has denied involvement.

Until a few weeks ago, the debate on Russia’s attacks on Europe was about the violent end of the spectrum: explosive-laden drones targeting a cargo plane in Leipzig, Germany; sabotage of railroad systems in Germany, the Netherlands, and Poland; drones over airports and military bases. These operations crossed into direct physical attacks and required capabilities that few actors possess. The past month shows the opposite end. A hoax bomb threat requires an email account and a few minutes, whereas the cost for the target is enormous: evacuations, bomb-disposal teams, aircraft diversions, fighter-jet scrambles, lost school days, and frightened parents. The authors of the “Message to the West” boasted of having caused widespread panic and forcing European authorities to spend a fortune on their emergency procedures.

This perfectly illustrates the asymmetry of hybrid threats. The defender cannot dismiss the threat because of its potential catastrophic impact, so every hoax triggers the full precautionary protocol. The attacker sets the tempo while the defender can only react and bear the cost.

A second feature makes this part of the hybrid war harder to counter. Schools, airports, and shopping centers in Europe receive their constant dose of empty threats from pranksters, students hoping to skip an exam, extortionists, and people with personal grievances. Each false alarm shows others how easy it is to cause disruption for free. On Wednesday, Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto predicted that such hoaxers will only multiply. Some of the threats against passenger flights claimed to come from the Male State, an anti-feminist movement banned in Russia. The claim of origin reads as mockery but also makes a point: No matter who is behind them, the hoaxes absorb resources and reinforce the perception of insecurity. For an attacker, each new campaign builds on the destabilizing effects of all previous ones.

This is why the low end of the attack spectrum is a useful reminder of what hybrid campaigns are for. Their purpose is psychological, the target is public opinion, and the objective is to generate confusion, fear, and distrust in institutions. A drone strike and a fake email serve the same purpose by different means. The first tests how far the threshold of attacks that Europe will tolerate without responding has moved. The second shows how little it takes to make citizens feel unprotected. Meloni put it plainly on Wednesday: The threats, she said, appear to be part of a strategy to generate alarm and concern.

The hoaxes also expose the attribution problem more starkly than sabotage does. Attribution is both a technical and a political issue. Pure data and forensic analysis rarely provide certainty about the sender. The senders of this month’s threatening emails have worn three masks: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards on Nov. 2, the Male State on Nov. 5, and a pseudonym evoking a long-dead Soviet leader since Nov. 6. Some of last week’s emails to airports came from an address at a public health network in the Colombian capital, Bogotá.

And even when the attack’s origin is clear, government leaders often lack the political will to name the attacker. The reason usually given is fear of escalation. A second reason is rarely admitted: Naming the attacker would mean telling their publics that Russia has already escalated a war against Europe, and that this war demands a response.

This creates a hard problem for policy. Against a threat with such disproportionate costs for the attacker and defender, reactive defense is a losing strategy. This is especially true given the fact that widely accessible technology makes these attacks ever cheaper to carry out at scale. The logical answer is deterrence, which means raising the cost and risk for the attacker. But deterrence rests on attribution, which will often be only partial.

A credible deterrent posture therefore requires a degree of political courage that European governments have so far avoided. It means saying, in advance and together: We may not know with certainty who is behind the next wave, but if it happens, we will impose costs based on the available evidence, even if that evidence is incomplete. This is a probabilistic standard of response, closer to how intelligence works than how courts work. It is uncomfortable for democracies bound by the rule of law and accustomed to standards of incontrovertible evidence. And it carries a risk of error. The alternative is the certain continuation of a campaign that costs an adversary nothing and undermines the target every time.

The posture must also be Europe-wide rather than national. A campaign that reaches Italian schools, Irish newsrooms, and Czech airports in the same week is designed to exploit divisions. A response that each country calibrates on its own invites the attacker to probe for the weakest link.

The final element is speed. Because hybrid campaigns rely on diffused costs and dispersed information, they have to be met with rapid information sharing. When thousands of schools receive the same threatening email at the same moment—and that fact is known within minutes by everyone concerned—then the threat largely diagnoses itself: It is a coordinated campaign, and the alarms are very likely false. Italy’s education minister, Giuseppe Valditara, said as much on Wednesday, noting that the sheer number of schools involved demonstrated how little credibility the threat had.

A similar logic applies to real attacks. When hackers took control of refrigeration systems in hundreds of French supermarkets in October and in stores across at least 11 European countries in early November, the pattern was the clue: It was a simultaneous, automated, and cross-border effort. A shared picture in real time turns hundreds of isolated emergencies into a single recognizable event. It speeds up the response, lowers the payoff for the attacker, and eases the attribution on which deterrence depends. At the European level, most of this civilian information sharing and coordination infrastructure does not yet exist.

In the last two months, we have witnessed two very different ways in which hybrid campaigns exploit free societies as targets for attack. At one end, Europe’s adversaries are testing how much violence it will absorb before it reacts. At the other, they show how cheaply European societies can be disrupted. Both types of attacks are aimed at citizens’ confidence that their institutions can protect them. Europe can answer at both ends, but only if it finds the unity and political will to do it.

Beniamino Irdi is a nonresident senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, the founder and CEO of HighGround, and a former Italian government official.

#5919. The Case for a Trump-Xi-Putin Summit

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. He is the author of Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come.

In just a few days’ time, U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin could be holding a three-way summit on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China. According to The Wall Street Journal, Putin floated the idea of a trialogue last month as an opportunity to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. No firm plan has yet been announced, but even the prospect of this meeting has provoked widespread consternation. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned against a repeat of the Yalta Conference of 1945, when U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill capitulated to Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s push for the Soviet Union to dominate Eastern Europe. U.S. Senator Chris Coons wrote on X that “There can be no talks about Ukraine’s future without Ukraine at the table, and there can be no real negotiations as long as Trump signals weakness and servitude to Xi and Putin at every opportunity.”

These worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats while turning his back on democratic allies. Should he sit down with Xi and Putin, he must avoid selling out European and Asian partners who will not be at the table. And given the three leaders’ headstrong personalities and competing national interests that pit the United States against what Xi calls a “no limits” partnership between China and Russia, the meeting may ultimately yield little progress on major issues.

Nevertheless, Trump would be right to join a summit with Xi and Putin. No U.S. president has ever held a trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia, and the proposed talks would break the ice and begin to normalize much-needed dialogue. Authoritarianism is not going away, so autocracies and democracies must learn not only to live comfortably alongside one another, but also to work together to tame geopolitical rivalry and tackle global challenges in an interdependent world. Americans will not find it easy to get along with the likes of Russia and China, whose political systems threaten the U.S. commitment to spreading democracy. But Trump is taking a bold step in the right direction by engaging with the heads of the world’s leading autocracies.

If he meets with Xi and Putin, Trump should aim low and focus on making meaningful, if limited, progress on a small number of core issues that could benefit from a three-way conversation: the flashpoints of the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine, and Iran, as well as arms control and strategic stability. But even if the summit yields no concrete results, it will nonetheless have been worthwhile. Trump, Xi, and Putin are paving the way for their successors to advance great-power cooperation across ideological lines and stabilize a fragmented world.

I have argued previously, including in a 2021 Foreign Affairs essay with Richard Haass, that a global concert—an informal steering group of great powers modeled on the nineteenth-century Concert of Europe—offers the best hope of curbing geopolitical competition and enabling collective action in a multipolar world. In addition to the United States, China, and Russia, a new concert would include India, Japan, the European Union, and representatives from Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Concerts sacrifice representation for efficacy and give only the geopolitically influential states that must be there a seat at the table. They set aside ideological differences and bring democracies and autocracies together to focus on international cooperation. Because concerts eschew binding, enforceable procedures in favor of informal consensus-building, they can succeed when formal institutions such as the UN Security Council are paralyzed and when the United States wavers in its commitment to rules-based multilateralism.

But the time has not come for a global concert. Concerts function effectively only when their members are committed to the territorial status quo, willing to exercise strategic restraint and pursue mutual benefits, and ready to settle disputes diplomatically. Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and Xi’s decision to back Russia have, for now, scuttled hopes that the great powers will normalize restraint and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Meanwhile, Trump’s “America first” statecraft shuns joint action and mutual gain in favor of unilateralism.

Yet even though Trump, Xi, and Putin are the wrong leaders at the wrong time to establish a great-power steering group that other major players would eventually join, Trump’s iconoclastic diplomacy sets a useful precedent. His Alaska summit with Putin last year and two summits with Xi this year were admittedly long on pageantry and short on substance. But by taking the controversial step of pursuing joint talks with the two leaders, Trump is widening the diplomatic Overton window and expanding what is politically possible for future U.S. presidents. Avoiding great-power conflict and taming a world in increasing disarray requires the United States to build constructive relations with both China and Russia. Trump deserves credit for starting a trialogue that his successors can carry forward.

If they meet in Shenzhen, Trump, Xi, and Putin should focus on easing tensions at key geopolitical flashpoints. The Korean Peninsula presents the best opportunity for the three leaders to collaborate. At the UN General Assembly in September, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung laid out an ambitious plan for normalizing relations with Pyongyang, including a proposal to replace the peninsula’s 1953 armistice with a “peace regime” that promotes “respect for each other’s systems and acknowledgement of our differences.” As part of that plan, Lee has advocated a phased approach to North Korean denuclearization, with an initial freeze on weapons development followed by gradual reductions in Pyongyang’s arsenal of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles until the peninsula is denuclearized.

Lee’s bold proposal could bring U.S., Chinese, and Russian interests into alignment. Trump has made it clear that he wants to de-escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula and is already seeking a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Beijing and Moscow are competing for influence over Kim, but both want a stable relationship between North and South Korea, so they may be willing to cooperate on proposals to halt nuclear weapons production and encourage talks between Seoul and Pyongyang. Trump, Xi, and Putin should aim to emerge from their meeting with a plan for advancing Lee’s peace agenda; jointly supporting a freeze on North Korean nuclear weapons development is a good place to start.

The prospects for progress toward ending the war in Ukraine are much dimmer, but not nonexistent. Trump should be striving to weaken Russia’s ability to sustain the war, but he has long resisted tightening sanctions on Moscow. He talks up potential business ventures with Russia, and, in recent weeks, even struck a deal with Putin to get more Russian diesel into global markets and waived a new round of congressional sanctions against Moscow. Trump evidently cares more about trying to bring down fuel prices than about curbing Russia’s ability to fund its war against Ukraine.

Xi has played along with Putin’s war against Ukraine so far, presumably because the conflict diverts U.S. attention and resources away from Asia, divides NATO, and allows Xi and Putin to cast themselves as leading a global resistance to Western hegemony. But when Xi and Trump met this May, the leaders agreed to pursue “a constructive relationship of strategic stability” between China and the United States, which Xi can advance by pressing Putin to de-escalate. As more Russians feel the effects of the war, the Kremlin may be newly receptive to such pressure. Ukrainian drone strikes are taking a significant toll on Russia’s oil sector and logistics networks, which means Russian citizens face mounting gas and commodities shortages. Meanwhile, some 35,000 Russian soldiers per month are losing their lives or sustaining severe injuries in eastern Ukraine, forcing Putin to consider the unpopular move of ramping up military mobilization. With no battlefield victory in sight, Putin has reasons to entertain a diplomatic off-ramp.

Trump and Xi can press Putin to accept a set of limited but consequential steps to de-escalate the conflict. These could include an agreement between Russia and Ukraine—brokered and monitored by Washington and Beijing—to end attacks on energy installations and infrastructure, civilian targets, and commercial shipping. Trump and Xi could also jointly press Putin to refrain from actions that could broaden the war, such as penetrating NATO airspace with Russian drones, sabotaging European infrastructure, and threatening to use nuclear weapons. This pressure, combined with the allure of improving diplomatic and commercial ties to the United States, may convince Putin to relent on at least some of these issues.

Trump could also use a trilateral summit to seek help extricating the United States from its war in Iran—a quagmire that has produced regional mayhem and soaring oil prices. As Tehran continues to issue maximalist demands and the war disrupts shipping through the straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, Trump needs an out.

Neither Xi nor Putin has yet been inclined to lend a hand. China is still buying Iranian oil and providing Tehran with military intelligence and dual-use items that end up in Iranian drones and missiles, and Russia is providing satellite targeting data, munitions, advanced drone technology, and logistical support. Both Beijing and Moscow are happy to see the United States mired in a conflict that is exacerbating divisions within the American electorate and fracturing NATO.

As a major energy exporter, Russia benefits from the spike in oil prices that the conflict has triggered, so pressing Putin to cease supporting Iran is likely a lost cause. But China is the world’s largest oil importer, and Beijing has a vested interest in lowering energy prices by stabilizing exports from the Middle East. Although China’s large oil reserves have buffered its economy from rising oil prices so far, those reserves have been significantly depleted. China’s crude oil imports have begun to climb again, leaving its economy exposed to high energy prices if the conflict drags on. And, as the world’s largest exporter of goods, China suffers from the dampening effect high energy prices have on global growth.

Xi might therefore be amenable to helping Trump end the war. Trump should ask Xi to stop, or at least slow, the flow of Chinese dual-use items to Iran. Washington’s naval blockade and financial and commercial sanctions on Tehran have already taken a toll on Iran’s economy and military supply chains. By cutting off Chinese technology shipments to Iran, Beijing could deepen this economic isolation and help convince Tehran to negotiate an end to the conflict.

Xi can also press Iran to drop its unrealistic demands for ending the war, including that the United States withdraw its forces from the Gulf and release frozen Iranian assets and remove economic sanctions. Washington may well be willing to offer economic relief, but only as part of postwar negotiation of a deal that reins in Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Xi can help clear the way for those talks by urging Iran to accept credible terms for ending the immediate conflict.

Beyond working to resolve current conflicts, Trump should promote future strategic stability by pursuing arms control negotiations with Putin and Xi. Every arms control agreement negotiated between Washington and Moscow has expired; their final nuclear pact, New START, ended in February. There are currently no caps on the American and Russian strategic arsenals and no regular inspections, data exchanges, or notifications of nuclear exercises. This nuclear free-for-all is particularly dangerous given Russia’s nuclear saber-rattling amid the war in Ukraine and the Kremlin’s fondness for provocations such as sending explosive-laden drones into NATO airspace.

In October, Trump appropriately proposed that a trilateral summit include a discussion of nuclear arms control. China has long resisted engaging in arms control talks, arguing that it should not have to limit its nuclear program when its arsenal is much smaller than that of the United States and Russia. But Beijing is rapidly expanding and modernizing its nuclear arsenal. The Pentagon projects that China will possess more than 1,000 operational warheads by 2030, putting it nearly in the same league as the United States and Russia, which have stockpiles of roughly 1,800 operational warheads each. With the uncertain trajectory of U.S.-Chinese relations, instability on the Korean Peninsula, and China’s tense relationship with Taiwan heightening the risk of conflict in East Asia, Beijing must be part of high-level nuclear arms control discussions.

Realistically, Trump can do little more than start this conversation and invite Xi and Putin to continue it in future trilateral negotiations led by teams of diplomats and arms control experts. In future talks, the three countries should discuss not only caps on nuclear weapons stockpiles but also military-to-military contacts, crisis management protocols, notifications of military exercises, counterproliferation, and other measures that can contribute to strategic stability.

Trump could add a host of other topics to the summit’s agenda, including trade, energy security, and AI regulation, but he should avoid a wide-ranging conversation that goes nowhere. He might, however, notch an easy win by proposing a three-way initiative in an area where cooperation is relatively straightforward—for example, a joint medical mission to the Democratic Republic of the Congo to help fight Ebola or a joint aid operation to deliver humanitarian relief to Yemen or Gaza. A concrete, public effort along these lines would show that trilateral dialogue can yield viable cooperation.

Yet Trump should guard against being so eager for a win that he lets Xi and Putin take advantage of him. The APEC summit takes place only two weeks after American voters dealt Trump and his party a historic rebuke in the U.S. midterm elections. The notoriously thin-skinned president could be tempted to make concessions to Beijing and Moscow to score a foreign policy breakthrough. He must avoid making a behind-closed-doors compromise on Ukraine that he then tries to force upon Kyiv and its European supporters. Similarly, he must hold the line on Taiwan even as he seeks Xi’s help on North Korea, Ukraine, and Iran. Otherwise, Trump will leave the trilateral meeting confirming the worst fears of those who foresaw a new Yalta in the making. Capitulating to Xi and Putin would alienate Washington’s allies, project American weakness, and erode global deterrence.

Trump must also carefully manage the optics of a trilateral summit. Putin is an indicted war criminal who continues to prosecute a ruthless war of aggression against Ukraine. It is far too soon to let him out of the penalty box. And although Washington is right to seek a good working relationship with Beijing, it is time for Trump’s “truly great friendship” with Xi to bear fruit. Trump must approach talks with sobriety and pragmatism, seeking to demonstrate that Washington, Beijing, and Moscow can work together to help promote global peace and stability.

A summit next week will not usher in a new era of great-power collaboration anytime soon. It may not even yield concrete deliverables. Still, the meeting would set a valuable precedent. Simply by sitting down with Xi and Putin, Trump will begin a much-needed trilateral conversation.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.

Two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, marked the undoing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid growing calls for his departure and a substantial drop in the company’s stock price.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Europe’s future involvement in Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and mounting political tensions in Indonesia.

Two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, marked the undoing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid growing calls for his departure and a substantial drop in the company’s stock price.

Huang has been seen as the face of the global artificial intelligence race. His company is the world’s leading producer of advanced semiconductor chips, making Nvidia a critical part of U.S. national security and a sought-after partner of China. Huang himself is among the world’s wealthiest people, with an estimated net worth of around $162 billion prior to his recent scandal.

Over the past two years, Huang has also become a close friend of U.S. President Donald Trump, whose administration has made advancing AI a cornerstone of its agenda. Notably, Huang successfully petitioned the White House last December to relax some restrictions on Nvidia sales to China in exchange for the U.S. government receiving a 25 percent cut of the profits.

But in just two weeks, Huang’s public image has collapsed. Late last month, the New York Times reported that a Chinese businesswoman believed to be spying for Beijing was in a “close relationship” with Huang. The alleged spy, Alice Huang, was an executive at a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed, which the U.S. Commerce Department began suspecting in 2024 of helping China to smuggle in Nvidia’s restricted AI chips.

Nvidia shares plummeted in the wake of the news, even as Beijing denied involvement. Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia’s 42,000-plus employees on Sunday.

However, the scandal didn’t end there. On Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang had had a separate affair with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare. That relationship may have violated the company’s code of conduct. Huang has not publicly acknowledged the second affair.

The dual allegations appear to have been enough to force Huang to step down. Huang has reportedly agreed to testify before Congress ahead of the U.S. holiday of Thanksgiving over the espionage scandal. And Nvidia finance chief Colette Kress has agreed to serve as interim CEO until a replacement is named.

Nvidia’s change in leadership, though, has yet to assuage global markets. Company shares plunged as much as 14 percent when trading opened on Thursday, extending a crisis that has already wiped out more than $1 trillion from Nvidia’s market value. Some initial gains were made later in the day but not enough to reverse the damage.

Nvidia’s board has said there is “no reason to believe” that Huang’s actions compromised U.S. national security or company secrets, but it has launched an independent investigation. And on Thursday, Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong issued a statement saying that the company takes its obligation to comply with U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously” and will work “constructively and transparently with the U.S. government.”

Trump, meanwhile, praised Huang on Thursday, writing on Truth Social that he had done a “fantastic job” with Nvidia.

A seat at the table. Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed on Thursday to allow European representatives to join the next round of direct Ukraine peace talks. Giving Europe a seat at the table marks a big win for Kyiv and Washington, which have both pushed for greater European involvement in negotiations. However, the concession could also spell trouble for future talks, as Moscow remains largely at odds with its European counterparts.

“We would very much like you, gentlemen, and the U.S. administration as a whole to work with your European allies so that they can finally make up their minds as to what they want: peace or war in Ukraine,” Putin told U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow on Thursday. At the same time, the Russian leader warned that any push for the deployment of European troops to Ukraine after a peace deal is inked would trigger renewed fighting.

Witkoff and Kushner will now head to Dublin for similar talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The potential of European involvement in the peace process will almost certainly be on the agenda, but Zelensky is also likely to bring up new reports of Starlink disruptions in Ukraine.

Zelensky on Thursday accused the U.S.-based company of placing speed restrictions on its Starshield military-grade services, affecting how its drone interceptors operate. The last time that such limits were detected, Zelensky resumed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries in direct opposition to Trump’s wishes. Kyiv and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had both accused the Trump administration of orchestrating that incident, which the White House denied.

Academic scandal. Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka submitted his resignation to parliament on Thursday in the wake of a scandal over his academic credentials. It is unclear when his departure will take effect; however, experts expect the incident to deliver another blow to the tenuous alliance between former President Joko “Jokowi” Widodo and current President Prabowo Subianto.

Calls for Gibran’s impeachment first intensified last month, when the country’s Constitutional Court found that the vice president did not possess the necessary credentials to hold power. In Indonesia, lawmakers must have a high school diploma to run for office. Gibran claimed to have finished grade 12 at a school in Australia, but the court ruled that the degree was not equivalent to an Indonesian senior high school certificate. Two weeks later, the country’s Supreme Court backed that ruling by revoking Gibran’s equivalency document.

Gibran was elected in 2024 largely as a symbol of the precarious truce between his father, Jokowi, and Prabowo. His removal could therefore further fracture that fragile alliance. Just last week, Indonesian authorities detained three senior police officials suspected of wiretapping the president and dozens of other prominent figures. Among those arrested was Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who was a known loyalist of Jokowi.

Gaza hospital attack. An Israeli airstrike targeted the main hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Younis overnight on Thursday, killing at least six people, including a teenager, and injuring at least 20 others. Locals reported two missiles damaging a building containing surgical wards at Nasser Hospital. The attack marked the latest violation of the region’s precarious Gaza cease-fire, which took effect in October 2025.

According to Israel’s military, the hospital strike was part of an operation targeting Muhammad Abu Ismail, whom Israeli forces described as the “commander of Hamas’s Khan Younis Brigade.” Israel claimed that Abu Ismail had turned Nasser Hospital into his headquarters and was using the facility as a base of operations. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of using civilian infrastructure as human shields. The militant group has denied doing so.

Since the Israel-Hamas war began in October 2023, Israeli troops have attacked Nasser Hospital at least seven times, according to hospital officials. The use of medical centers for military purposes and the targeting of such sites are both considered violations of international law. “Gaza’s health facilities are lifelines for its ​people,” World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote on X on Thursday. “They must be protected. They must never be militarized or attacked.”

The Finnish Embassy in Canberra temporarily closed its doors on Tuesday for a one-day internal planning and staff sauna event. However, what was meant to be a routine disruption instead appeared to upend the internet, with a deluge of memes jokingly bemoaning the closure. Local swimming pools offered their services for those suffering, a Dutch esports league complained about the lockout, and even American Airlines unveiled a snap sale on flights to Europe for emotional support.

The embassy, meanwhile, took the public’s outcry in stride. “After 24 harrowing hours, international expressions of grief and an unprecedented outpouring of solidarity, the Embassy of Finland in Canberra has officially reopened,” the facility posted on social media on Wednesday, marking the event with a ribbon-cutting ceremony.
